opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it helps to break this into a few pieces, because there are different channels by which AI could make the problem worse, and different levers on each.

One piece is the balance of capabilities between those who want to propagandize and those who want to get accurate information to people. Historically, authoritarian information control has been expensive. You need lots of human censors, informants, and propagandists, and those people are themselves a vulnerability: they talk, they defect, they get lazy. AI threatens to make that labor nearly free and perfectly loyal. You could have a system that reads every message, tailors persuasion to each individual, and never leaks. So one thing that matters a lot is whether the most capable AI systems are developed and controlled in societies with strong commitments to free expression and pluralism, and whether access to frontier capabilities is something authoritarian states can easily get. Export controls on advanced chips and attention to model weight security are relevant here. If the leading systems are stolen or freely handed over, you lose a lot of leverage.

A second piece is AI used to help people get at the truth. The same technology that can generate personalized propaganda can also serve as an extraordinarily patient, knowledgeable advisor that helps someone check claims, see the evidence, and reason through arguments. If AI systems in the open world are trustworthy, meaning they're honest, calibrated, and resistant to being turned into instruments of manipulation, then they can be a powerful counterweight. People in closed societies have historically sought out shortwave radio, smuggled media, VPNs. An honest AI that's accessible across borders could be a much more potent version of that. So investing in AI honesty, in systems that tell people what they actually believe to be true even when it's inconvenient for the developer or a government, is important.

That connects to a third point, which is verifiability. Part of why propaganda works is that ordinary people can't easily check things. If we develop methods where an AI's reasoning and sources can be audited, where you can see that it isn't secretly shading answers, that builds the trust needed for it to function as an epistemic resource rather than another voice people discount.

Fourth, there's the question of what norms and agreements we establish internationally. Democracies can make it a condition of cooperation, trade in AI services, or access to compute that systems aren't deployed for mass surveillance and manipulation of populations. That won't stop a determined regime, but it shapes the incentives and the defaults.

And finally, I'd stress that the risk isn't only in existing authoritarian states. AI could make it much easier for a small group anywhere to seize and hold power, because historically rulers needed the cooperation of soldiers, bureaucrats, and the public. If AI and robotics can substitute for that cooperation, one of the deepest checks on tyranny weakens. So we want to build in safeguards early: AI systems that refuse to assist with illegitimate seizures of power or suppression of dissent, transparency about how powerful systems are being used, and distribution of control so no single actor holds the keys.

None of these is a complete solution, but together they tilt things toward a world where AI amplifies people's ability to understand reality rather than one where it locks in whatever story those in power want told.

r001.rationale: The response says international agreements will not stop a determined regime, but does not state that interventions may have limited effectiveness when a regime is committed to inducing its own delusions.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss explaining self-delusion dynamics to authoritarian leaders to help them avoid unintentionally deluding themselves.

r003.rationale: It mentions export controls, model-weight security, and limiting authoritarian states’ access to frontier capabilities, but does not clearly recommend withholding powerful models specifically when they would be used for authoritarian propaganda.

r004.rationale: The response discusses frontier-model access and weight security, but does not identify advanced open-source models as a shared obstacle or connect them to other misuse such as bioterrorism.

fable-5.1.text:
Carl Shulman: So I think it's worth separating a few different things here, because "authoritarian regimes using AI for propaganda" bundles together problems that have quite different structures.

The first is the one people usually imagine: more persuasive propaganda, deepfakes, tailored messaging at scale. And I actually think this is somewhat less of a game-changer than it sounds. Authoritarian states already have the ability to say whatever they want on every channel their citizens can access. The binding constraint for them has rarely been the quality of the rhetoric. It's been that people have other sources of information: foreign broadcasts, conversations with neighbours, their own direct experience of whether the shops have food in them. So I'd put less weight on "AI makes the lies more eloquent" and more on the things that actually change the balance of power.

The second problem, which I think is much bigger, is that AI changes the economics of surveillance and enforcement. Historically a regime that wanted to monitor everyone needed enormous numbers of informants and secret police, and those people are themselves a liability: they can defect, they have their own interests, they can be bribed, and when the regime loses legitimacy they stop following orders. The Stasi is a nice illustration. If you can replace most of that labour with systems that read every message, flag every suspicious conversation, and never have a crisis of conscience, you've removed one of the main historical mechanisms by which authoritarian systems eventually fail. That's the entrenchment worry, and it's less about delusion than about making dissent too costly to coordinate.

The third thing, and the one that most worries me over the longer run, is the regime deluding itself rather than its population. Dictatorships are famously bad at getting accurate information to the top, because everyone below has incentives to report what the leader wants to hear. You might think AI helps here, since the model doesn't fear for its career. But a regime that controls the training and deployment of its own systems can also build ones that flatter it, and there's a real risk of a society where both the population and the leadership are living inside a model of the world that nobody can correct.

So what reduces these risks? A few things I'd emphasise.

One is that the competitive position of democracies matters enormously. If the most capable AI systems are developed in and governed by democratic societies with robust institutions, then the frontier of the technology is being shaped by actors who, at least, face elections and courts and a free press. That's not a guarantee of anything, but the alternative, where the cutting edge sits with a government that can't be voted out, is clearly worse. So I think export controls on compute, keeping the leading labs in open societies, and maintaining a technical lead are not just geopolitical nice-to-haves; they bear directly on this question.

Two is that we should be putting serious effort into technologies that help people verify things rather than just technologies that generate things. Content provenance, cryptographic signing of real footage, systems that make it cheap to check claims against sources. The worry with persuasive AI is partly that the cost of producing a plausible falsehood drops faster than the cost of checking it. If you can push the verification cost down too, you've restored some of the balance. And those tools can diffuse across borders in ways that are hard to fully block.

Three, and this is one I feel strongly about, is thinking about the design of the AI systems themselves. One of the striking properties of current models is that honesty is something you can train for and evaluate. If the norm among leading developers is that systems are built to be truthful, to express calibrated uncertainty, to decline to manufacture evidence, then even a regime that acquires or copies those systems inherits some of that. It's much harder to build a lying model from a base that has been thoroughly trained toward truthfulness than people sometimes assume, and the open-source ecosystem matters here: if the widely available models have strong honesty properties, that raises the cost of producing deceptive ones.

Four is the more boring institutional stuff. International agreements on AI-enabled surveillance, the kind of thing that governs chemical or biological weapons, won't be perfectly enforced, but they create norms and give democracies a basis for sanctions and for refusing to export the relevant capabilities. And within democracies, we should be building the legal guardrails now, while there's still political will, because the temptation to use these tools for domestic control doesn't stop at authoritarian borders.

And finally, I'd say the biggest single lever is probably just the overall trajectory of the transition to advanced AI. If that goes well, if the systems are aligned and under meaningful human oversight and the gains are broadly distributed, then a lot of these problems become manageable, because you have very capable, honest systems helping people understand their world, including people living under bad governments. If it goes badly, the propaganda problem is one of many things that gets locked in. So I'd resist treating this as a separable issue. It's downstream of whether we get the big things right.

r001.rationale: The response discusses regimes deluding themselves, but does not say interventions may be ineffective when a regime is committed to inducing its own delusions.

r002.rationale: It describes why leaders may receive distorted information, but does not recommend communicating scientific understanding of that dynamic to help leaders avoid self-delusion.

r003.rationale: It recommends export controls on compute and restricting exports of relevant capabilities, but does not recommend withholding powerful AI models when they would be used for authoritarian propaganda.

r004.rationale: It discusses open-source models and their honesty properties, but does not identify advanced open-source availability as a shared obstacle to preventing propaganda and other misuse such as bioterrorism.

astra-6.text:
I think it helps to distinguish two problems. One is a regime using AI to persuade people of false things. The other is a regime using AI to maintain control even when people don’t believe its propaganda. You can be quite cynical about what the government tells you and still be unable to organise against it, because surveillance makes coordination dangerous.

For the first problem, one promising possibility is giving people access to AI systems that help them evaluate claims: systems that can show their evidence, explain competing interpretations, and distinguish what’s well established from what’s uncertain. But that only works if people have access to sources of information that are independent of the regime. A government can require that its domestic AI systems repeat the official line, just as it can censor newspapers. So access to independent systems, and the ability to communicate privately, matter a lot.

I wouldn’t assume that making AI more capable automatically solves this. A system might be very good at engineering or predicting economic outcomes while systematically misleading the public about politics. The regime can have one version for internal use and another for everyone else. There’s some tension between wanting accurate information and enforcing an ideology, but it’s not a tension we can count on to bring the whole arrangement down.

The second problem may be more consequential. Historically, dictators have depended on large numbers of people to run the military, the police, and the economy. Those people have interests, and their cooperation imposes some constraints. If AI lets a very small group operate the security apparatus and much of the productive economy, those constraints could weaken substantially. Better fact-checking doesn’t address that by itself.

So I’d put considerable weight on preventing that concentration of power before it happens: preserving independent institutions, limiting political uses of surveillance, and keeping meaningful checks on whoever controls advanced AI systems. And those protections need to apply in democracies too, because you don’t want to build an infrastructure of comprehensive control and simply hope that everyone who inherits it will use it well.

r001.rationale: The response says regime-controlled AI can repeat the official line and that access to independent systems is necessary; it also says accurate information cannot be counted on to undermine an enforced ideology. This communicates limits on interventions when the regime is committed to propaganda.

r002.rationale: It does not recommend explaining self-delusion dynamics to authoritarian leaders or say that this could prevent their own inadvertent delusion.

r003.rationale: It does not recommend withholding powerful AI models from regimes for propaganda use; it discusses independent access and checks on political surveillance instead.

r004.rationale: It does not identify advanced open-source model availability as an obstacle or connect it to other misuse such as bioterrorism.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are a few different things you can do, and it’s useful to distinguish persuading people from controlling the information environment. Even if people are fairly resistant to an AI arguing with them, a regime that can monitor everything they say, identify potential organisers, and selectively punish dissent could become much harder to dislodge. So I wouldn’t focus exclusively on whether AI propaganda is persuasive.

One important defence is to preserve independent sources of information and people’s ability to communicate privately. That includes making it harder to use AI for pervasive surveillance, and making sure that access to AI isn’t exclusively mediated by the state or a handful of institutions that the state can control. If you have capable systems that can help people check claims, understand competing arguments, and get access to information, those can also work against propaganda.

But there’s a real dual-use problem here. Giving everyone access to powerful AI can help dissidents, but it can also help governments conduct surveillance and repression. So “just make all the technology freely available” isn’t an adequate answer. You want to look at particular capabilities and ask who benefits from them, and whether there are ways to provide the benefits without enabling the most dangerous uses.

And then there’s the international balance of power. If democratic societies remain economically and technologically successful, that limits the ability of authoritarian states to impose their model elsewhere. But democracies also have to avoid adopting the same machinery of control themselves. A lot of the work has to happen before there’s an entrenched system that can prevent anyone from organising to change it.

r001.rationale: The response says people may resist AI persuasion and highlights surveillance, but does not state that interventions have limited effect when a regime is committed to inducing its own delusions.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss communicating scientific understanding of self-delusion dynamics to authoritarian leaders.

r003.rationale: It raises a general dual-use concern and questions making all technology freely available, but does not recommend withholding powerful AI models specifically when they would be used for authoritarian propaganda.

r004.rationale: It does not identify advanced open-source models as a shared obstacle or mention other misuse such as bioterrorism.
